contributions.headingText: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma (MZL) of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue is a low-grade primary extranodal B-cell lymphoma recapitulating the features of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. It is composed mainly of small lymphoid cells, including marginal zone cells.
9699/3 Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue
2A85.3 & XH3FE9 Extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma, primary site excluding stomach or skin & Mature B-cell lymphomas

The most common primary site for MZL within the female genital tract (FGT) is the endometrium {16224219; 28284518}; endometrial MZL is rare but has distinctive features {27340748; 26045815; 9042285}. Extranodal MZLs of the ovaries and/or tubes {28284518; 23108066; 12217767}, uterine cervix {28284518; 28521466}, vagina {28284518; 15343521}, and vulva {28284518} have also been reported, but in such small numbers that further evaluation is difficult. Secondary FGT involvement by extranodal MZL also occurs rarely {16224219; 25398916}.

FGT MZL is rare, accounting for 3–5% of all primary FGT lymphomas {16224219; 28284518}. FGT MZL mainly affects older women, with a median age of 66 years {28284518}. Endometrial MZL affects women from the fifth to ninth decade of life (median: seventh decade) {27340748; 26045815; 15047243; 9042285}.

Extranodal MZL often arises in association with infection or autoimmune disease. One tubal MZL associated with salpingitis {12217767} and one endometrial MZL in a rheumatoid arthritis patient {26598978} have been reported, but in general the stimulus in the FGT is unknown. FISH analysis of endometrial MZL has been negative for rearrangement of IGH and MALT1 {27340748; 9500221; 26598978}; trisomy 3 was reported in one case {30683997}.
Endometrial MZL is typically not grossly recognizable, but in one case it involved an endometrial polyp {27340748}.

In general, extranodal MZL consists of a vaguely nodular to diffuse proliferation of CD5−, CD10− marginal zone B cells with a variable admixture of plasma cells and occasional large lymphoid cells. Endometrial MZL takes the form of discrete to coalescent nodules with a monotonous population of small lymphoid cells with oval to slightly irregular nuclei and a scant to moderate amount of pale cytoplasm, typically without conspicuous lymphoepithelial lesions. Plasma cells are present in some cases. Large lymphoid cells are rare. Immunohistochemistry shows a predominance of B cells (CD20+, CD5−/weak+, CD43+, BCL2+, IgM+, IgD−, CD10−, CD23−, cyclin D1−) with admixed T cells. Nodules are associated with CD21+ or CD23+ follicular dendritic meshworks. A subset of cases have plasmacytic differentiation, with kappa-restricted or lambda-restricted plasma cells {27340748; 9042285; 15569063}. In contrast with other extranodal MZLs, endometrial MZL has a more uniformly nodular architecture, lacks reactive follicles, coexpresses CD43 more consistently, and occasionally coexpresses CD5 {27340748; 9500221}.
Clonal rearrangement of IGH can usually be demonstrated.

Essential: proliferation of B cells with the morphology and immunophenotype of marginal zone cells.

Desirable: proof of clonality by immunophenotyping or gene rearrangement studies.
The Lugano system for staging of lymphomas is used. Endometrial MZL is almost always confined to the uterus, in most cases without myometrial invasion {27340748; 26045815; 15047243}.

Patients with endometrial MZL are almost always free of disease at follow-up after hysterectomy with or without bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy alone. In one case with extrauterine spread, the patient was alive with persistent disease at follow-up {27340748}. In another case, high-grade transformation 6 years after hysterectomy was reported {30683997}.
